text: The Ga arrived on this coast as two groups who had travelled together: one from Ile-Ife in present-day Nigeria, one from the region of the present-day Congo. At La, the leader of the first, Odoi Atsem, became Mantse (chief), and the leader of the second, Numo Nmashie, became Mankralo, his second-in-command. Around 1710 a feud between them threatened civil war. Rather than fight, Nmashie moved east, bought land from the Nungua Mantse, Afote Okley, and founded Teshie. He did not make himself chief. He appointed Nii Trebi, kept the role of Mankralo, and set up the town's first quarters, Krobo, Agbawe and Klemusum, entrusting the Lakpa deity to Klemusum. Settlers soon came from La, Nungua, Tema, Accra and Prampram. The town is still remembered in a Ga accolade, “Gonti ni ashiii see anmoo kpo”, recalling a time when the whole Ga State fought under the Teshie Mantse (translation to be confirmed with an elder).

text: Adjetey places the founding earlier, in the late 1600s, and describes Teshie as a garrison town, settled after civil conflict broke out in neighbouring La. Both dates are shown here; we don't pick a winner.
